title: AI model
short: The program that writes Copilot’s answers.
body: The program that writes Copilot’s answers. It learned patterns from huge amounts of text and code, and predicts a useful reply to what you send. Copilot lets you choose between several models.
analogy: A very well-read colleague who has never seen your project.

title: Reasoning model
short: A model that thinks step by step first: slower and pricier.
body: A model that works through a problem step by step before it answers. Better on genuinely hard problems, but slower, and each request costs more.
analogy: Asking a colleague to sit down and think it through, rather than answer off the top of their head.

title: Prompt
short: What you type to Copilot.
body: What you type to Copilot: a question, a task or an instruction. The clearer it is, the fewer rounds you need.
analogy: The brief you give a contractor.

title: Context
short: Everything the model sees when it answers.
body: Everything Copilot sends to the model with your prompt: the chat so far, files you attach, instruction files and tool results. The model only knows what is in the context. It has no other memory of your project.
analogy: A whiteboard. Whatever is written on it is all the model can see.

title: Token
short: The chunk of text models read and bill in.
body: The unit models read, and the unit usage is measured in. A token is a chunk of text, often part of a word: in English, a token is roughly three-quarters of a word on average. Code and symbols usually take more.
analogy: Syllables. Long or unusual words take several.

title: Context window
short: The most context a model can take at once.
body: The most context a model can take in one request, measured in tokens. As a chat nears the limit, older parts get summarised or dropped and answers get worse.
analogy: The size of the whiteboard.

title: Chat history
short: Every prompt and reply in the current chat.
body: Every prompt and reply in the current chat. It is sent again with each new prompt, which is why long chats get slower and cost more.
analogy: Rereading the whole email thread before every reply.

title: Agent
short: Copilot acting, not just answering.
body: A Copilot role that doesn’t just answer. It works out the steps, edits files, runs commands and checks the results, repeating until the task is done or it needs you.
analogy: A junior developer you supervise, rather than a search engine.

title: Tool
short: An action an agent can take.
body: An action an agent can take, such as reading a file, searching the code, running a terminal command or fetching a web page. Whatever a tool returns is added to the context.
analogy: The agent’s hands and eyes.

title: Hallucination
short: A confident answer that is wrong.
body: A confident answer that is wrong, such as a function, setting or package that doesn’t exist. Models predict likely text. They don’t check facts unless a tool, a test or you do.
analogy: A colleague bluffing instead of saying “I don’t know”.

title: AI credits
short: How Copilot usage is billed.
body: How Copilot measures usage: each request costs credits based on the model and the tokens used. Bigger models and bigger contexts cost more.
analogy: A phone plan billed by the minute, where some numbers cost more to call.

title: Auto (model)
short: A setting that picks a suitable model for each request.
body: A choice in the model picker. Copilot routes each request to a suitable model and saves pricey reasoning models for hard problems. Paid plans get a small discount for using it.
analogy: Letting the sat-nav choose the route instead of always taking the motorway.

title: Inline suggestion
short: Grey ghost text offered as you type.
body: The grey “ghost text” Copilot offers as you type in the editor. Press Tab to accept it, or keep typing to ignore it.
analogy: Autocomplete on your phone, for whole lines of code.

title: Inline chat
short: A small chat box that opens right where your cursor is.
body: A chat box that opens in the editor or terminal, right at your cursor, and works on what you selected. Small context, quick answers.
analogy: Asking the person next to you, instead of booking a meeting.

title: Slash command
short: A shortcut you type after /, such as /clear.
body: A shortcut you type in the chat box after a forward slash, such as /clear to start a new chat or /plan to plan a task. Your saved prompt files run the same way.
analogy: Keyboard shortcuts, but typed as words.

title: # mention
short: Type # to attach a file, the errors or other context.
body: Type # in the chat box to attach exactly the context you mean: a file, your selection, the errors in the Problems panel or the last terminal command.
analogy: Stapling the relevant page to your question.

title: @ participant
short: Type @ to ask a specialist, such as @terminal.
body: Type @ in the chat box to send your question to a specialist that knows one area well, such as @vscode for editor settings or @terminal for shell commands.
analogy: Asking for the expert in that area by name.

title: Instruction file
short: Team rules Copilot adds to every request.
body: A Markdown file in your repo, such as .github/copilot-instructions.md, whose rules Copilot adds to requests automatically. You write the team’s conventions once instead of in every prompt.
analogy: The onboarding notes you hand every new starter.

title: Prompt file
short: A saved prompt in the repo that anyone can run with /name.
body: A Markdown file ending in .prompt.md, saved in the repo, that holds a prompt you use again and again. Anyone on the team runs it by typing / and its name.
analogy: A saved email template.

title: Front matter
short: Settings between --- lines at the top of a Markdown file.
body: A short block of settings between two --- lines at the very top of a Markdown file. In prompt and instruction files it sets things like the name, the model or which files the rules apply to.
analogy: The label on the front of a folder.

title: applyTo glob
short: A file pattern that says which files some rules are for.
body: A file pattern, such as db/migrations/**/*.sql, set as applyTo in an instruction file’s front matter. The rules are only sent when matching files are in play.
analogy: A label saying “for the kitchen only”.

title: Custom agent
short: An agent role you define, with its own rules and tools.
body: An agent role saved as a .agent.md file, with its own instructions and a chosen set of tools, such as a reviewer that can read code but never edit it. Pick it from the Agent picker.
analogy: A job description for one particular task.

title: Agent skill
short: A folder of steps and files the agent can follow on request.
body: A folder with a SKILL.md file that describes a repeatable procedure, plus any scripts or templates it needs. Run it with / and its name.
analogy: A recipe card with the ingredients clipped to it.

title: Compaction
short: Shrinking the chat into a short summary.
body: Replacing a long chat history with a short summary, so it takes fewer tokens. /compact does it when you ask; VS Code also does it automatically when the window fills.
analogy: Wiping the whiteboard but keeping a sticky note of the key points.

title: Checkpoint
short: A restore point Copilot saves before each chat request.
body: A restore point that VS Code saves before each chat request. Restoring one rewinds the files and the chat, but not commands the agent has already run.
analogy: The undo history in a document, but per request.

title: Tool approval
short: The moment you allow or deny what the agent wants to do.
body: Before the agent runs a command or uses a tool, VS Code can ask you first. You allow it once, for the session, or deny it. Auto-approve skips the question.
analogy: A contractor asking before knocking down a wall.

title: Sandbox
short: A fenced-off space where commands can’t reach everything.
body: A fenced-off space for the commands the agent runs, limiting which files and network addresses they can reach. In VS Code it is a preview setting.
analogy: A playpen: the agent can play, but can’t wander off.

title: MCP server
short: An add-on that gives the agent extra tools.
body: An add-on that gives the agent extra tools, such as access to a database, an issue tracker or a browser. MCP stands for Model Context Protocol.
analogy: A plug-in adapter that lets the agent use one more system.

title: Content exclusion
short: An admin setting that hides chosen files from Copilot.
body: A setting that Business and Enterprise admins use to keep chosen files away from Copilot. It does not cover Agent mode, so the agent can still read them.
analogy: A “staff only” sign on a door that one visitor ignores.

title: Code referencing
short: Shows where a suggestion matches public code, and its licence.
body: When a suggestion matches code in a public repository, code referencing shows you where it came from and under which licence, so you can decide whether you may use it.
analogy: A citation at the bottom of an essay.

title: Cloud agent
short: A Copilot agent that works on GitHub’s servers, not your laptop.
body: A Copilot agent that works on a task on GitHub’s servers, then opens a pull request for you to review. You hand it a GitHub issue or delegate from VS Code chat.
analogy: Sending a task to a colleague in another office, who sends back the finished change.

title: Diff
short: A before-and-after view of a change.
body: A view of exactly what changed in a file: removed lines and added lines. Reading the diff is how you check Copilot’s work before you keep it.
analogy: Tracked changes in a Word document.

title: Repository
short: The project folder and its full Git history.
body: The project’s folder and its full history of changes, kept by Git and usually shared on GitHub. Often shortened to repo.
analogy: A shared drive that remembers every version of every file.

title: Commit
short: A saved snapshot of your changes, with a message.
body: A saved snapshot of your changes in Git, with a short message saying why. Small commits make a bad change easy to undo.
analogy: A save point in a game.

title: Pull request
short: A proposed change that teammates review before it’s merged.
body: A request to merge your changes into the main code, where teammates (and Copilot code review) can read the diff, comment and approve. Often shortened to PR.
analogy: Handing a draft to an editor before it goes to print.

title: Terminal
short: The command line inside VS Code.
body: The command line built into VS Code, where you run builds, tests and Git. Agents can run commands there too, which is why approvals matter.
analogy: Talking to the computer in typed sentences instead of clicks.

title: CI check
short: An automatic build and test run on every pull request.
body: An automatic build and test run that GitHub (or another service) does on every push or pull request. A red check means something failed.
analogy: A spell-checker that runs before anything is printed.

title: Merge conflict
short: Two branches changed the same lines; someone must choose.
body: When two branches change the same lines, Git can’t combine them on its own and asks you to choose. Copilot can propose a resolution for you to review.
analogy: Two people editing the same paragraph of a shared document.
